The Australasian shoveler (Spatula rhynchotis) exhibits a characteristic incubation strategy typical of dabbling ducks, with eggs maintained at a consistent temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] throughout the developmental period. Under these thermal conditions, hatching occurs after approximately 24 days [ab = approximately 24 days], a duration that aligns with the incubation periods documented for other members of the at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] genus Spatula. Newly emerged ducklings emerge from the calcareous egg at a modest initial wet weight of 43.2 grams [Ww0 = 43.2 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves required to sustain the altricial nestling through its first days of exogenous feeding. This neonatal body mass is comparatively low relative to the ultimate adult size the birds will achieve, underscoring the rapid growth trajectory characteristic of Anatidae during the early nestling phase. The downy chicks are brooded intensively by the female for the first week post-hatch, during which time they rely entirely on residual yolk nutrients before transitioning to active foraging under maternal guidance, a critical period that sets the foundation for subsequent developmental milestones.

Once the nestling chicks begin to thermoregulate effectively, the metabolic demands of the brood increase substantially. Basal metabolism in adult Australasian shovelers has been measured at 473.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 473.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under standard thermoneutral conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a rate that is consistent with the moderate body size and foraging ecology of this filter-feeding species. This resting metabolic rate represents the energetic baseline against which all other physiological activities are calibrated, including the considerable costs of feather synthesis during the fledging period. The pin-feathered chicks begin to develop flight feathers at approximately five weeks of age, with first flight achievement, or fledging, recorded at 49 days after hatching [tx = 49 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime. Field records, however, indicate that the full fledging period can extend to 91-119 days in natural settings, a variability that likely reflects differences in food availability and parental provisioning rates across wetland habitats.

Sexual maturation in the Australasian shoveler follows a predictable trajectory under the thermal conditions typical of temperate Australasian environments, where birds experience a body temperature approximating 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] during active metabolic periods. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal development and gametogenesis, is reached at 147 days after hatching [tp = 147 days after hatching], a duration that positions this species among the later-maturing dabbling ducks at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay in reproductive activation is ecologically meaningful, as it allows juvenile birds to complete their somatic growth and build the lipid reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of egg production and courtship. The period between fledging and the attainment of sexual maturity represents a critical life-history window during which young birds refine their foraging skills and establish familiarity with potential breeding sites, factors that directly influence their future reproductive success. Male and female shovelers follow similar timelines in gonadal development, though subtle differences in hormone profiles appear as they approach reproductive viability.

The maximum lifespan of the Australasian shoveler has been estimated at approximately 16.6 years [am = approximately 16.6 years] from field banding records and captive studies conducted at a standard body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity places the species within the upper range documented for Anatidae, a pattern consistent with its relatively slow life-history pace and moderate investment in annual reproductive output. Comparative analyses among dabbling ducks suggest that lifespan is positively correlated with body mass and inversely related to annual fecundity, a trade-off that shapes demographic strategies across the clade. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations have been recovered from band returns in New Zealand and southeastern Australia, providing robust evidence for a maximum recorded longevity of about 6,059 days [am = about 6,059 days] when converted from years at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This extended lifespan allows individuals to accumulate breeding experience across multiple seasons, potentially enhancing reproductive success late in life.

Reproductive output in the Australasian shoveler is characterized by a single annual breeding event, with females laying between 6 and 14 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 6 and 14 eggs per clutch] during the spring-summer breeding season. The species produces exactly one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a frequency typical of migratory and temperate-nesting dabbling ducks that face a limited window of optimal resource availability. The first successful breeding event typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when maintained under the thermoneutral body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], meaning most individuals do not reproduce until their second calendar year. This deferral of first reproduction aligns with the pattern observed in other mid-sized Anseriformes, where young birds prioritize body condition and territory establishment over immediate breeding. The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult females is 619 grams [Wwi = 619 grams], while adult males attain a slightly larger asymptotic body mass of 641 grams [Wwi = 641 grams], a moderate sexual size dimorphism that is correlated with male-male competition for access to females on the breeding grounds.
